results.description:
Growth is inhibited by acid soils, pH 6.0 and lower.
 Peas are hardy, but seed germination is delayed when soil temperatures are below 40°F. Warmer soils (up to 75°F.) will speed germination and emergence. Plant growth is favored by intermediate temperatures (65° - 70°F) while flowering is accelerated by long, cool days. [...] Pre-germination is another method of starting seeds. Sprouting the seeds before they are planted gives them a head start before being planted in the garden. By closely controlling temperature and moisture you can achieve a higher and quicker rate of germination. [...] Days to maturity: 50 to 70 from direct seeding.
 Fertilizer needs: Heavy user of nitrogen (peas fix little nitrogen). Incorporate fertilizer before seeding. Growth is inhibited by acid soils, pH 6.0 and lower. Refer to Fertilizing Vegetables for details.
 Approximate yield: 3 to 5 pounds per 10-foot row.

# Soil Penetration Resistance as a Soil Health Indicator

Soil penetration resistance is the force required to move a specially-tipped metal rod through the soil. The soil penetration resistance value is comparable to the force required for a plant root to grow through the soil. Penetration resistance is also used to identify soil density. [...] A penetrometer is used to measure soil penetration resistance. The two types of penetrometers that are frequently used are static and dynamic penetrometers.

requirements.missing: No supplied document distinguishes whole fruit versus cleaned seed for Pisum sativum (green pea). Documents s0–s3 address Cicer arietinum (chickpea), not the requested crop; pea documents (s4–s11) discuss seeds generically without the required whole-fruit vs cleaned-seed distinction.

Temperature thresholds for Pisum sativum appear in s5–s11 (e.g., minimum ~40 °F, optimum ~75 °F), but no source provides (a) a target soil-moisture percentage for emergence, nor (b) a validated soil-crust measurement method (penetrometer reading or visual rating scale) specific to pea germination. Penetrometer documents (s12–s14) address subsurface compaction, not surface soil crust.

Sources are US university extensions (UMN, NDSU, UW-Madison, OSU, Penn State, USDA NRCS) with °F temperatures, but none report soil moisture as a percentage (by volume or gravimetric) nor tie temperature thresholds to specific calendar dates. The required moisture and date-bound geography are absent.
